questions.q: Per this lesson, when is a declarative Case Assignment Rule actually the better choice over an Apex trigger?
options: For simple, field-based routing logic that declarative rules can already express through clicks, without needing cross-object lookups or callouts
Never — Apex is always preferable for Case routing
Only when the org has fewer than 10 Cases total
Case Assignment Rules can't route Cases at all, so Apex is always required
questions.explain: This lesson is explicit that for simple field-based routing, declarative Case Assignment Rules are genuinely the right tool — Apex earns its place once the logic needs something rules can't easily express.

questions.q: Why does the handler use `Map<String, String> QUEUE_NAME_BY_ORIGIN` instead of a long if/else chain?
options: Maps execute faster than if/else statements in all cases
Apex does not support if/else chains longer than two conditions
A Map scales more easily as routing rules grow, since adding a rule means adding one entry rather than another branch to a growing chain
Maps are required by Salesforce for any trigger that sets OwnerId
questions.explain: Centralizing routing rules as Map entries treats the logic as data, which scales more cleanly than a growing if/else chain as new routing cases are added.

questions.q: Why can this trigger set `c.OwnerId` directly without a separate update statement?
options: OwnerId cannot be set in Apex at all, so this code has no actual effect
Because the handler is declared without sharing
Because Group queues bypass DML entirely
Because it's a before-insert trigger, which can modify Trigger.new directly and let the platform's own save operation persist the change
questions.explain: A before trigger can modify fields on Trigger.new directly, and those changes are saved as part of the record's own insert — no extra DML statement is needed, unlike in an after trigger.

questions.q: Why does the handler query the Group object for queue Ids instead of hardcoding them as literal Id strings?
options: Group records cannot be queried from Apex
Hardcoded Ids are environment-specific and can silently break when deployed to a different org, per Lesson 28's best practice
Querying is required because Group has no DeveloperName field
It has no real benefit; it's purely stylistic
questions.explain: Looking up queue Ids by DeveloperName at runtime avoids the hardcoded-Id problem from Lesson 28, since a literal queue Id from one org's sandbox is not guaranteed to match production.

questions.q: What happens to a new Case with `Origin = 'Email'`, which is not a key in QUEUE_NAME_BY_ORIGIN?
options: It falls back to the General_Triage queue, via the FALLBACK_QUEUE_NAME default
The trigger throws an unhandled exception and the insert fails
Its OwnerId is left completely unset
It is automatically routed to Tier_1_Support by default
questions.explain: The ternary check falls back to FALLBACK_QUEUE_NAME whenever the Case's Origin isn't a key in the routing map, so an 'Email' origin routes to the General Triage queue.
